messages.author: e4aec126ff1dca22
messages.subject: New 2d stat/geom thoughts
parts:
Hi all!

I was playing around with some tessellation stuff yesterday and thought that, in addition to looking cool, some of the same visuals could be useful in a variety of situations.  Maybe someone who has some time would want implement them as stats/geoms.  

Without further explanation, see code below, which culminates in the attached plot.  The stats/geoms I refer to are pretty obvious.

Cheers
david.

library(ggplot2)
library(deldir)
library(scales)
library(reshape2)
library(plyr)






# make fake points
n <- 50
k <- 4
mat <- cbind(rnorm(n), rnorm(n))
df <- as.data.frame(mat)
names(df) <- c('x','y')
qplot(x, y, data = df)


# convex hull
hull <- chull(df)
hullPointsIndices <- c(hull, hull[1])
hullPoly_df <- df[hullPointsIndices,]

qplot(x, y, data = df) +
  geom_polygon(data = hullPoly_df, colour = 'red', fill = 'red',
    alpha = I(1/10), size = 1)







# triangulate
xrng <- expand_range(range(df$x), .05)
yrng <- expand_range(range(df$y), .05)
deldir <- deldir(df, rw = c(xrng, yrng))

qplot(x, y, data = df)  +
  geom_segment( # polygons would be nicer...
    aes(x = x1, y = y1, xend = x2, yend = y2), size = .5,
    data = deldir$delsgs, colour = 'red', alpha = .5
  )
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
# triangulate with polygons
trilist <- unclass(triang.list(deldir))
tridf <- melt(trilist, id.vars = c('x','y'))[,c(3,1:2)]
names(tridf) <- c('tri','x','y')
  
qplot(x, y, data = df)  +
  geom_polygon(
    aes(x=x, y=y, fill=factor(tri)), 
    data = tridf, colour = 'black', alpha = .5
  ) +
  scale_fill_discrete(guide = FALSE)
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
# voronoi
qplot(x, y, data = df)  +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = x1, y = y1, xend = x2, yend = y2), size = .25,
    data = deldir$dirsgs, linetype = 2
  ) + 
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0,0)) 
  
  
  
  
  
# voronoi with polygons
tilelist <- unclass(tile.list(deldir))
tilelist <- lapply(tilelist, function(l){
  data.frame(x = l$x, y = l$y)
})
tiledf <- melt(tilelist, id.vars = c('x','y'))[,c(3,1:2)]
names(tiledf) <- c('tile','x','y')

ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y), data = df)  +
  geom_polygon(
    aes(x = x, y = y, fill = factor(tile)),
    data = tiledf, colour = 'black', alpha = .5
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_fill_discrete(guide = FALSE) +  
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0,0)) 
  
  

  
  
  
  
# all together now!  
ggplot(aes(x=x, y=y), data = df)  +
  geom_polygon(data = hullPoly_df, colour = 'red', fill = 'red',
    alpha = I(1/10), size = 1) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = x1, y = y1, xend = x2, yend = y2), size = .25,
    data = deldir$delsgs
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = x1, y = y1, xend = x2, yend = y2), size = .25,
    data = deldir$dirsgs, linetype = 2
  ) + 
  geom_point(size = 5.75, alpha = .75) +
  geom_text(aes(label = 1:n), size = 3, colour = 'green') +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0,0))   
  
  
  
  
ggplot(aes(x=x, y=y), data = df)  +
  geom_polygon(
    aes(x = x, y = y, fill = factor(tile)),
    data = tiledf, alpha = .5
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = x1, y = y1, xend = x2, yend = y2), size = .25,
    data = deldir$delsgs
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = x1, y = y1, xend = x2, yend = y2), size = .25,
    data = deldir$dirsgs, linetype = 2
  ) + 
  geom_polygon(data = hullPoly_df, colour = 'red', fill = NA,
    alpha = I(1/10), size = 2) +  
  geom_point(size = 5.75, alpha = .75) +
  geom_text(aes(label = 1:n), size = 3, colour = 'green') +
  scale_fill_discrete(guide = FALSE) +    
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0,0))

messages.subject: Re: New 2d stat/geom thoughts
parts:
Hi David,

It's a very useful stat to have for sure. I remember a discussion with
Hadley and the author of deldir. There's a similar function
panel.levelplot.voronoi in latticeExtra (with the option to switch to
a faster package for the Delaunay calculation).

Unfortunately, last time I looked (last week) this deldir() function
was atrociously slow on reasonable data sets (~1e5 points, I'm looking
at electric field distributions in the output of a finite element
modelling software that uses such irregular tesselations).

There's also the recent interface to the C Triangle library on
r-forge: https://r-forge.r-project.org/R/?group_id=1077
I was in contact with the author when he started the project, and I
think he added some functionality to output the tesselation in a
format suitable for plotting.

Keep me updated if you're working on it!

Thanks,

baptiste

PS: The geom + stat is in the wiki wishlist:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/wishlist---feature-requests

> was atrociously slow on reasonable data sets (~1e5 points, I'm looking

Sure, different implementations may be faster. I only looked at the one in the tri... (I don't remember off the top of my head) package; but I went the other way after 10 min or so because it seemed overly complicated. For example, I couldn't figure out how to extract the triangles as polygons in any easy way, just line segments which isn't as useful in ggplot2.

On the other hand, how useful would the plots be with tons of points? I just ran it for 5k points (~30k triangles/tiles), and it could do it fine with a couple seconds lag; but I'm working on a very good machine. Attached are the tiles (ggplot2 stained glass!). Do you have an application where the visualization of the tiles/triangles is useful at that scale?

For the FEM, that would be a very useful feature I would think, and one that didn't immediately come to mind. Maybe there could a thinning in very high density regions where many points/triangles/tiles are which wouldn't be displayed effectively.

messages.author: e4aec126ff1dca22
messages.subject: Re: New 2d stat/geom thoughts
parts: > Just out of curiosity, what sort of data is this for and what does the plot mean?

Well, the data in the email is fake (obviously). But the Voronoi diagrams, for example, are useful in spatial stats as well as things like knn. Baptiste's example of the finite element method is a cool one, and is actually general to any kind of mesh not just FEM applications.

Or the convex hull. That's essentially the same as geom/stat_density2d, with the exception that it isn't calculating a contour of the density but it's convex support. So you could have a stat_chull, or geom_chull, or maybe both as in density2d (at this point the division seems pretty blurry...), or perhaps it'd depend on the contour stuff; I'd just have to look at it.

Does that help?

david.
